overview: The Vakatakas were a major Deccan dynasty with different ruling branches. Much of their history and famous Ajanta patronage predates this map’s imported 500 to 600 interval. Its broad outline is a rough regional approximation, not a reliable frontier or proof that Vakataka government continued everywhere until 600.

periods.title: Early rulers and branches
periods.summary: Vakataka power expanded and divided between related royal lines.

periods.title: Queens, grants and monuments
periods.summary: Gupta connections and regional patrons shaped fifth-century political and cultural life.

periods.title: Changing regional power
periods.summary: Vakataka rule ended at different times; exact final sequences remain debated.

items.text: Pravarasena I helped turn an emerging dynasty into an important regional power. Later eastern and western branches followed different political paths. Nagardhan belonged to the eastern royal landscape, while the western line is closely associated with Ajanta’s later flowering. One family name therefore covers several courts and changing territories.

Prabhavatigupta’s Pune charter introduces her as the daughter of Gupta emperor Chandragupta II, queen of Vakataka ruler Rudrasena II and mother of crown prince Divakarasena. Her own name stands at the centre of the order granting a village. The document makes a royal mother’s governing authority visible, alongside the family connections through which that authority was expressed.

Patronage supported different religious communities. At Mandhal, archaeologists found a substantial brick temple platform and nearby sculptures associated with Vishnu and Shiva. Ajanta’s Buddhist monasteries drew support from ministers and other powerful patrons. These remains show a varied religious landscape; a ruler’s personal devotion does not tell us what every household believed.

sections.title: Homes, food and small traces of everyday life

items.text: Nagardhan’s excavated neighbourhoods preserve rebuilding over time. An area spanning late Satavahana and Vakataka phases contained brick walls and a drain; another building phase had a rammed floor strengthened with crushed brick and lime. These practical surfaces tell a less glamorous story than palace treasure: people needed durable rooms and ways to move water.

Nagardhan’s wider excavated collection includes spindle whorls, bangles, terracotta animals, wheels and gaming pieces. Spindle whorls helped turn fibres into thread, while the ornaments and play objects bring work and leisure into the picture. The collection spans several occupation phases, so it cannot supply a perfectly dated inventory of one Vakataka family’s cupboard.

Animal bones preserve tiny dramas. The excavation report describes a young sheep or goat jaw chewed by a carnivore and a cattle ankle bone with punctures characteristic of a dog. Some other bones bore cutting or burning marks. These are traces of handling, meals and scavenging across the sampled deposits, not a complete menu for the dynasty.

Charred seeds from Nagardhan include rice, wheat, barley, millets and pulses, alongside crops such as cotton and flax. The published Early Historic group spans about 300 BCE to 600 CE, including times before Vakataka rule. It reveals a long-lived mixture of foods and useful plants. A burnt seed is a small accident that can become a large clue for an archaeologist.

A clay sealing excavated at Nagardhan carries part of Prabhavatigupta’s name and a conch emblem. Fingerprints survive along its side, while marks on the back suggest it had been attached to a consignment. The authors think accidental firing helped preserve it. Someone’s ordinary squeeze of wet clay survived far longer than the package it once helped secure.

sections.title: Villages, documents and a Sanskrit voice

items.text: The Pune copperplate grant exempted its donated village from certain demands, including supplying flowers and milk. The charter also transferred fiscal rights to the recipient. Such details expose everyday obligations behind royal generosity: officials and religious establishments depended on goods and revenues produced by villagers. The grant changed who could claim particular resources; it did not abolish taxation throughout the kingdom.

The early-fifth-century Pune charter opens with Sanskrit “jitam bhagavatā”, translated by V. V. Mirashi as “Victory has been attained by the Bhagavat!” Here Bhagavat refers to Vishnu. This is scholarly Roman transliteration of a Southern Brahmi inscription, not its original letter shapes. The charter dates itself to Prabhavatigupta’s thirteenth year and names its engraver, Chakradāsa.

sections.title: Ajanta: paintings, rooms and drinking water

items.text: Ajanta was already a Buddhist site centuries before the Vakatakas. Its later building phase added remarkable rock-cut architecture, sculpture and wall paintings during the fifth and sixth centuries. Painted stories of the Buddha’s previous lives brought people, animals, buildings and dramatic encounters into monastic spaces. The achievement belongs to many makers and patrons, rather than one king painting an entire hillside.

Cave 16 was donated by Varahadeva, a minister of King Harishena. Its monastery had sixteen cells arranged around a hall, and elephants carved near the entrance. The plan helps us imagine residents moving between smaller rooms and shared space. Grand religious art and the practical need for somewhere to stay belonged to the same building.

Monks also needed drinking water. The space now numbered Cave 18 originally served as a water cistern before becoming a passage between neighbouring caves. At Cave 6, sixteen pillars supported a ceiling that also formed the floor of the upper monastery. Water storage and structural support were essential parts of making a cliffside community work.

sections.title: Political endings and places that continued

items.text: Dating Ajanta’s later work remains a scholarly debate. Walter Spink proposed a tightly compressed fifth-century sequence ending in a patronage crisis after Harishena’s death; other specialists allow a longer period. An unfinished cave cannot by itself provide an exact fall date for every Vakataka branch. The map’s endpoint of 600 should not settle that argument.

The disappearance of Vakataka royal power did not erase the region’s communities. Nagardhan’s archaeological sequence includes medieval occupation as well as earlier phases. Buildings, settlement patterns and rulers changed over time. The site’s continuing history is a useful reminder that the end of a dynasty and the end of a town are different events.

ending.text: The Vakataka branches lost power around the late fifth and early sixth centuries, through a regional sequence whose details remain uncertain. Later rulers, including the Kalachuris, controlled parts of their former territory. No single securely established conquest explains the end of every branch, and 600 is this map’s endpoint rather than a documented fall year.
